extracted.intended_audience: readers of political theory, constitutional designers, educated public interested in forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Critically assess what constitutional form best preserves liberty and public good, weighing mixtures of assemblies, senates, and executives and their practical effects in historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitution / balance of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: “The people being in their assemblies, tempered by another coequal assembly, and an executive coequal with either, are the best keepers of their liberties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a constitution that mixes popular assemblies, a senate (or second chamber), and an independent executive so each checks the others. Examples offered: Roman mixture (tribunes tempering senate) and the superiority of a threefold legislature for large nations. Anti-pattern: single, undivided popular sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single popular assembly as sole sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: A single representative or collective assembly (untempered democracy) can be the worst keeper of liberty because it is prone to throw away liberties and morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware constitutions that concentrate legislative, executive, and judicial power in one popular body; such forms risk rapid demagoguery, moral decline, and the loss of liberty. Historical cautions in the text point to Athens-style excesses, mob violence, and the Florence/Cofimo examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive power from popular hands
rubrics_metrics.description: “Provided you keep the executive power out of their [the people’s] hands entirely...Without this the rich will never enjoy any liberty, property, reputation, or life, in security.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutions to keep executive authority distinct from transient popular majorities to prevent executive capture by electoral demagogues and protect minority rights/property. Anti-pattern: placing full executive/judicial power under untempered popular control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate or upper council as guardian of tradition and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate functions as “a living repertory of all the history, knowledge, interests, and wisdom of the commonwealth,” preserving national maxims and guiding prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an institutional body that holds long-term memory and experience (insulated from short-term popular pressures) to act as a check and mentor for the polity. Guidance advises that such a body be 'guarded from ambition' and balanced by popular negatives and executive checks. Anti-pattern: eliminating an experienced deliberative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: People must have a meaningful share plus a decisive negative
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let the people have a full share, and a decisive negative; and, with this impregnable barrier against the ambition of the senate on one side, and the executive power with an equal negative on the other, such a council will be found the patron and guardian of liberty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should give the people robust participation (e.g., electoral power, representation) while also granting them a structured veto or negative on other branches—balancing popular influence with institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property and rights of wealth-holders as part of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is essential to liberty that the rights of the rich be secured; if they are not, they will soon be robbed...and thus neither the liberty or property of any will be regarded.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit protections for property and security of wealth as a constitutional objective, since failure to secure property invites cycle of robbery and social breakdown. Historical examples used to warn against unchecked redistributive popular policies (abolition of debts, division of goods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional capacity to manage luxury and wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution must be “capable of preserving liberty among great degrees of wealth, luxury, dissipation, and even profligacy of manners”; a threefold balance is recommended for large, wealthy nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a form suited to the nation's scale and prosperity: small, frugal republics may function with simpler checks, but populous, wealthy nations need more complex balances to restrain the corrupting effects of sudden wealth and luxury. Anti-pattern: simple democracies in rich societies where instant emulation and luxury corrupt offices and elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent exposure of governors to the baits of luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal government is where governors are least exposed to the baits and snares of luxury; excessive exposure makes them susceptible to corruption to win popular favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design office-holding, remuneration, and electoral incentives to reduce pressure on officeholders to indulge and pander; examples warn that in democracies aspirants must outdo each other in dress, entertainments, and generosity to secure votes, thereby prostituting executive and legislative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use law and institutions, not mob violence, to vindicate liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let legal liberty vindicate itself by legal punishments and moral measures; but mobs and massacres are the disgrace of her sacred cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize formal legal remedies, courts, and sanctions to defend rights rather than relying on popular vengeance or extralegal reprisals. Anti-pattern: encouraging or tolerating mob justice (De Witts, other massacres cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against demagoguery and popular intolerance of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncontrolled popular majorities will not long tolerate freedom of inquiry, debate, or writing; popular enthusiasms may render criticism dangerous and lead to outrage, insults, and violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure constitutional protections for speech, debate, and dissent; build institutional buffers so that popular passion cannot readily extinguish inquiry or punish critics. Anti-pattern: arrangements where popular assemblies instantly suppress dissent and inﬂict vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent, purely successive annual assemblies that enable clientelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual successive assemblies chosen by the people may lead to a majority following a powerful patron and can make a popular leader absolute (Florence/Cofimo example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the frequency and structure of elections—too frequent or uncontrolled successive assemblies can be captured by charismatic patrons; incorporate institutional checks (upper chamber, executive negatives) to prevent consolidation of power by a single leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional form should scale to territory and population
rubrics_metrics.description: The threefold balance’s excellence lies in being capable of governing a great nation and large territory, whereas other balances exist only in small ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a constitutional design that worked in small city-states is appropriate for larger, more complex nations; prefer institutional designs that can operate effectively at national scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain luxury by laws, manners, and mixed government
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury should be restrained by morality and law; mixed government is the best means to manage luxury where it otherwise leads to corruption and tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine legal prohibitions, cultural norms, and institutional checks (mixed constitution) to limit excesses. Anti-pattern: relying solely on exhortation or simplistic governance forms that lack capacity to enforce restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving people undivided supreme offices/assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving the people the whole executive and judicial power, or even the whole undivided legislative power, is not the way to preserve liberty; such undivided supremacy invites abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent concentration by ensuring different branches and chambers share authority and provide mutual negatives; explicitly avoid constitutional arrangements that vest all supreme offices or assemblies in a single popular body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design upper chamber (senate) with safeguards against ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate, 'guarded from ambition', and balanced by people's negatives and executive checks, serves as patron and guardian of liberty; but it must be constrained against ambition itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create selection, tenure, and accountability mechanisms that insulate the senate’s institutional memory and prudence while preventing its capture by private ambition (e.g., fixed terms or protections combined with checks). Anti-pattern: a powerful but unchecked aristocratic council.
